title: What should training accomplish? — Directed adaptation
text: Start with the adaptation you want, then justify each part of the program. Specificity asks whether training directly creates the desired adaptation or prepares something that will enable it later. Repeated exposure to a sufficiently consistent stimulus allows technical skill and tissue adaptations to accumulate. Constantly replacing the main exercises or rep ranges can interrupt that process. The authors discuss a possible preparatory-to-myofibrillar sequence of hypertrophy; treat this as their proposed mechanism, not as a measured timetable for an individual. A light practice squat may support future growth by improving technique even if it is not itself a demanding growth stimulus. This is different from assuming every difficult activity builds the muscles you want. In a training log, give each activity a direct-growth, support, or other-goal role.

title: What should training accomplish? — Size and strength overlap, but goals differ
text: Start with the adaptation you want, then justify each part of the program. A larger muscle can support greater force production, but maximal lifting performance also depends on skill, neural coordination and familiarity with heavy loads. A heavy single may improve expression of strength while providing little total hypertrophy work for its fatigue cost. The book therefore rejects treating a one-repetition record as the main objective of a muscle-growth phase. Conversely, progressing repetitions with stable technique over several mesocycles can be useful indirect evidence of growth. It is not proof: motor learning and altered range of motion can also raise performance. Compare like with like, and read performance alongside body measurements, photographs and recovery observations over an appropriate timescale.

title: What should training accomplish? — Key takeaways
text: Justify training by its relationship to the desired adaptation. Stable exposure supports learning and adaptation; strength records are not direct muscle measurements.

title: Concurrent activities and opportunity cost — Four questions about compatibility
text: Judge interference by overlap, stimulus type, energy cost and fatigue. Ask whether an added activity uses the same structures, asks those structures to adapt in a different way, consumes substantial energy, or produces considerable damage and fatigue. More overlap with a conflicting stimulus generally increases interference with an exclusive hypertrophy goal. Long-distance running and quadriceps growth compete more directly than a short, easy recreational activity and arm growth. The book ranks endurance and combat sports as less compatible with maximal hypertrophy than technique-based sports or low-impact hobbies. This is a goal-specific ordering, not a judgment of their value for health or enjoyment. Multiple goals are legitimate; account for their tradeoffs instead of expecting to maximize all of them simultaneously.

title: Concurrent activities and opportunity cost — Make tradeoffs visible
text: Judge interference by overlap, stimulus type, energy cost and fatigue. Create a weekly map of muscle loading, demanding sessions, and genuine recovery days. A sport practice can load the same joints and supporting muscles as a gym session even when it is not counted as a lifting set. Energy expenditure also affects whether eating supports growth or turns an intended surplus into maintenance. Worked example: a trainee wants larger legs while preparing for a distance race. Removing all running would violate the race goal. Instead, identify which goal has priority in the current block and reduce expectations or training demands for the other. This is an original decision example applying the book’s compatibility framework, not a quantified interference formula.

title: Concurrent activities and opportunity cost — Key takeaways
text: Other training consumes time, energy and recovery resources. Evaluate compatibility relative to stated priorities.

title: Build a needs analysis — Needs, strengths and weaknesses
text: Turn preferences and physique demands into explicit priorities. First describe the desired outcome. Competitive physique standards and a hobbyist’s personal preferences need not be the same. Then compare current strengths and weaknesses with that outcome and rank muscle groups by priority. A program that always trains a lagging muscle last may not match its stated priorities. Allocate more fresh training time to priority muscles while preserving enough work elsewhere. Beginners generally have room to train the whole body productively; advanced lifters may need specialization. Avoid prescribing advanced specialization merely because a novice dislikes one body part. The practical question is what limits useful progress, not which routine looks most professional.

title: Build a needs analysis — Compounds, isolations and nutrition
text: Turn preferences and physique demands into explicit priorities. Compound movements stimulate several muscles efficiently, while isolations can add local work when a synergist or systemic fatigue limits compounds. Neither class is universally superior. Excessively narrow exercise selection can miss regional or biomechanical actions and concentrate repetitive stress; excessive isolation can waste time and broader stimulus opportunities. Diet supports the training goal. The source discusses adequate protein at approximately 1 g per lb of body mass per day (about 2.2 g/kg/day ) and sufficient energy for growth. This is the authors’ general nutrition context, not a personal dietary prescription. Growth, maintenance and fat-loss phases create different recovery conditions; later chapters return to those differences.

title: Build a needs analysis — An original priority map
text: Turn preferences and physique demands into explicit priorities. Needs-analysis finding Program implication Check in the log --- --- --- A muscle is a genuine priority Give it fresh attention and appropriate dose Does it always end up last? A muscle is already developed enough Preserve it with an appropriate maintenance emphasis Is extra work consuming recovery? Several goals matter State a current block priority Is the promised outcome realistic? A compound is limited by a support muscle Adjust technique, exercise mix or complementary isolation Which structure actually ends the set? This original decision table combines the source’s needs analysis and under/over-application examples; it is not an automatic prescription. The hamstrings illustrate complementary actions: knee flexion and hip extension are not trained identically by leg curls and hip hinges. Likewise, a press and a fly do not cover precisely the same pectoral action or range. The nutrition discussion additionally proposes 4–6 reasonably spaced meals with daily protein spread fairly evenly. This is a source-specific example supporting the broader point that diet can change the result of the same program. It is not a necessary meal schedule for every learner.

title: Build a needs analysis — Key takeaways
text: Make muscle priorities explicit before choosing exercises. Use compound and isolation movements as complementary tools.

title: What makes a set stimulative? — Tension and motor-unit recruitment
text: Mechanical tension, recruitment, effort and range of motion work together. Overload has two components: a session must be challenging enough now, and the challenge must increase as adaptation changes capacity. This does not require lifting above a maximum. Mechanical tension is central: a motor unit combines a motor neuron with the muscle fibers it controls, and higher force demands generally recruit larger units under the size principle. Heavier loads recruit demanding units directly; lighter loads can recruit more of them as fatigue builds near failure. A maximal single supplies high tension but little repeated exposure. Hypertrophy therefore depends on the combination of load, useful volume and effort, not on maximizing one variable while ignoring the others.

title: What makes a set stimulative? — Signals and proxies are not the same
text: Mechanical tension, recruitment, effort and range of motion work together. The source considers metabolite accumulation and cell swelling alongside tension as candidate contributors to growth, while recognizing uncertainty in their independent causal roles. Mind–muscle connection, pump and post-session disruption can help locate the stimulus, but none proves that a muscle will grow. Severe soreness can consume recovery resources and impair subsequent training. Movement velocity and range of motion modify the stimulus. Controlled eccentrics, useful stretch and an appropriate contraction can train a broad range of motor units. Do not shorten range just to claim load progression. The source favors a full, safe, goal-appropriate range; forcing additional range that breaks technique or causes joint pain does not meet that criterion.

title: What makes a set stimulative? — Effective repetitions: a model, not a binary switch
text: Mechanical tension, recruitment, effort and range of motion work together. The source calls repetitions near failure more effective because high-threshold units contribute a greater share of force, but explicitly notes that earlier repetitions are not useless. Counting only the last five repetitions as if all previous work had zero effect can produce misleading equivalences. Two submaximal hard sets and one failure set can contain a similar count of “effective reps” without being equivalent training. Its stimulus diagrams show a threshold region, diminishing returns and eventually excessive-dose costs; their smooth curves are conceptual. They do not provide a measured equation for kilograms of new muscle. The soreness diagram makes the same distinction: some disturbance can accompany useful training, while severe damage competes with adaptation for recovery resources. The authors’ proposed preparatory hypertrophy mechanisms include cellular fluid and glycogen changes, structural protein expansion and satellite-cell nuclear contribution before fuller contractile growth. This is presented as a hypothesis explaining why abrupt changes may lose some training momentum, not as a proven mandatory two-stage schedule.

title: What makes a set stimulative? — Key takeaways
text: Overload means an adequate and progressively challenging stimulus. Pump, burn and soreness are observations, not direct growth measurements.

title: Load, effort and volume landmarks — Read load and effort separately
text: Understand useful ranges without turning them into universal prescriptions. Absolute load is the resistance lifted. Relative load expresses it as a fraction of that exercise’s 1RM. Relative effort is expressed here as repetitions in reserve (RIR): an estimate of how many additional full, technically acceptable repetitions remain. A set of ten can be easy or near failure depending on the person and load. The book describes a broad working range of approximately 30–85% 1RM when sets are close enough to failure, usually 5–0 RIR . These are source ranges with assumptions, not precise cutoffs. Very light loads require many repetitions and can be limited by discomfort; very heavy loads constrain total work and raise fatigue costs. Average effort around 2–3 RIR is an author guideline, not a prediction of growth.

title: Load, effort and volume landmarks — Four volume landmarks
text: Understand useful ranges without turning them into universal prescriptions. Landmark Meaning in the source framework --- --- MV Enough training to maintain current muscle MEV Enough to begin robust measurable growth MAV The currently most productive volume region MRV The greatest volume from which recovery permits continued productive training These are individual, muscle-specific, phase-dependent estimates. MAV is not a fixed set target to chase forever. The authors often organize accumulation from near MEV toward MRV, followed by reduced training. Continuing to add sets after recovery and performance fail is not productive overload.

title: Load, effort and volume landmarks — Hard sets versus tonnage
text: Understand useful ranges without turning them into universal prescriptions. The source usually counts hard sets within useful load and effort ranges to compare hypertrophy volume. Tonnage is sets × repetitions × load , with units such as kg; it omits displacement and is not mechanical work. Work would require force and distance, with units of joules. Neither metric alone measures muscle growth. Example: 3 × 10 × 40 kg and 5 × 5 × 48 kg both total 1,200 kg of external load moved. They differ in sets, effort and recruitment conditions, so equal tonnage does not establish equal stimulus. Compare the same exercise with consistent technique and record RIR and recovery as well.

title: Load, effort and volume landmarks — Tempo and useful range: boundaries and exceptions
text: Understand useful ranges without turning them into universal prescriptions. The source separates eccentric, transition (amortization) and concentric phases. It describes broadly similar hypertrophy across controlled durations up to about 3 seconds per phase and about 9 seconds for a whole repetition, while allowing naturally slower near-failure repetitions. These are author interpretations of the evidence, not rigid speed limits. Pauses can improve control or alter loading requirements without being inherently more anabolic. Useful range has three upper constraints: technical breakdown, extra motion that shifts demand away from the intended muscle, and painful or unsuitable joint positions. There are also deliberate exceptions to full-range defaults. A peak-hold row can emphasize scapular retractors in the upper portion; an advanced trainee can sometimes justify a partial when it clearly improves target limitation and SFR. These exceptions do not justify accidental shortening as load increases. Original comparison: if one week’s press touches a consistent endpoint and the next stops several centimeters earlier, the heavier load is not an equivalent performance comparison. Record the changed technique before interpreting adaptation.

title: Load, effort and volume landmarks — Key takeaways
text: Load, effort and volume describe different dimensions. Landmarks move with recovery conditions and adaptation.

title: Load, effort and volume landmarks — Compare hard sets and tonnage
text: Distinguish a volume bookkeeping measure from a hypertrophy outcome. The source counts useful hard sets and explains why mathematical volume cannot alone establish growth equivalence. Arithmetic demonstration only. Inputs represent consistent external-load units and the same exercise standard. No growth, recovery, medical or individualized training prediction. RIR and technique are not inferred. At 3 sets, 10 reps and 40 kg, tonnage is 1,200 kg. At 5 sets, 5 reps and 48 kg it is also 1,200 kg; equal tonnage does not prove equal stimulus. Verify tonnage = sets × reps × kg and relative load = kg ÷ 1RM kg × 100; reject nonpositive 1RM and nonfinite inputs; exercise bounds are educational controls, not safety prescriptions.

title: Load, effort and volume landmarks — Explore absolute and relative load
text: Calculate a percentage of a specified exercise 1RM and separate it from RIR. The source uses relative load and relative effort as separate variables; neither predicts growth by itself. Arithmetic demonstration only. Inputs represent consistent external-load units and the same exercise standard. No growth, recovery, medical or individualized training prediction. RIR and technique are not inferred. A 60 kg load with a 100 kg 1RM is 60% 1RM. The same external load is 75% when 1RM is 80 kg. RIR still requires a separate observation. Verify tonnage = sets × reps × kg and relative load = kg ÷ 1RM kg × 100; reject nonpositive 1RM and nonfinite inputs; exercise bounds are educational controls, not safety prescriptions.

title: Choose a set structure — Straight sets and down sets
text: Use ordinary and advanced methods for a clear reason. Straight sets repeat a movement with enough rest for the target muscle to be the limiting factor again. Before the next set, consider the target muscle, synergists, overall readiness and breathing. A fixed short rest is counterproductive if cardiorespiratory fatigue stops the set before the intended muscle is challenged. The authors make straight sets the foundation of most programs. Down sets reduce load after earlier sets so later work stays within the chosen repetition range. They are not the same as short-rest drop sets. Keeping the same exercise saves additional warm-up time and preserves comparability; adding a new movement is useful only if its benefits justify the transition and its different demands.

title: Choose a set structure — Advanced methods and their limitations
text: Use ordinary and advanced methods for a clear reason. Method Purpose and limitation --- --- Giant sets Reach a total-repetition target; weekly performance is harder to compare Non-overlapping supersets Pair unrelated or antagonist muscles to save time; systemic fatigue can still interfere Pre-exhaust supersets Isolation then a compound for the same target; changes the limiting factor and increases local fatigue Myoreps Short-rest mini-sets after an initial hard set; best when the target muscle, not breathing, limits work Drop sets Reduce load between short-rest sets; track the reductions rather than improvising endlessly Blood-flow restriction Can make light loads effective; requires appropriate equipment, screening and qualified guidance Advanced methods are tools, not guaranteed upgrades. Highly systemic exercises are often poor choices for very short rests. Novel methods still need progression, recoverability and a clear role.

title: Choose a set structure — Track the details of the method
text: Use ordinary and advanced methods for a clear reason. In the source’s myorep example, an initial 10–20-repetition set at about 0–2 RIR is followed after a few breaths by smaller 5–10-repetition bouts. Drop sets add load reductions to a similar short-rest idea. They target efficiency and local fatigue; their suitability depends on the target, not on how much discomfort they produce. Pre-exhaust pairs use an isolation first so the same muscle can become limiting in the following compound. The source’s Table 5.1 proposes accounting heuristics: a conventional straight or down set counts as one; a giant-set bout, drop set or occlusion set may be counted as about 2/3 of a straight set for the primary target; a myorep mini-set may similarly count as 2/3, sometimes one when fatigue response is high. A non-overlapping superset counts one set for each target, while the pre-exhaust pair is roughly two sets, or about 1.5 in the authors’ finer estimate. These fractions are author bookkeeping conventions, not verified biological conversion constants. If you use such a convention, label it and keep the method, rest, load and range consistent. Do not combine an unlabelled fractional estimate with ordinary set counts and assume precise equivalence. Blood-flow-restriction setup is intentionally not taught as a self-application procedure here.

title: Choose a set structure — Key takeaways
text: Rest long enough to challenge the intended muscle. Select advanced methods for a specific benefit and track their costs.

title: Progress without exhausting the runway — Estimate stimulus conservatively
text: Combine sets, repetitions, load and RIR using actual response. The authors combine perceived target-muscle challenge, pump and disruption into a raw stimulus magnitude (RSM) score. Each is rated 0–3, giving 0–9 in total. Their MEV estimator regards roughly 4–6 as a useful starting signal, but this is a coaching heuristic, not a validated assay of hypertrophy. RSM is specific to a person and muscle; it should not rank different people. Use several observations together. No soreness does not demonstrate no stimulus, and a large pump does not demonstrate sufficient tension. Compare equal set counts after allowing time to learn an exercise. A high RSM may also come with excessive fatigue, which the next chapter addresses.

title: Progress without exhausting the runway — Progress from response, not enthusiasm
text: Combine sets, repetitions, load and RIR using actual response. Start near an estimated effective dose. If soreness resolves well before the next exposure and comparable performance improves, modestly adding sets may be reasonable. If recovery occurs just in time and targets are met, hold sets steady. If soreness overlaps and performance falls, investigate fatigue instead of adding work. Performance constraints take precedence over chasing soreness. Progress load or repetitions enough to stay within the chosen range and effort trajectory. A possible accumulation moves from more RIR toward less, while preserving later training. Do not sharply increase load, sets and failure proximity together just because each can progress separately. For giant sets, use total repetitions plus other comparable straight sets to monitor fatigue; for drop sets and myoreps, record rest and loading conditions.

title: Progress without exhausting the runway — Avoid both weak and excessive overload
text: Combine sets, repetitions, load and RIR using actual response. Junk volume adds fatigue without meaningful contribution to the intended adaptation: it may be insufficiently specific, too far from failure under light loads, or beyond useful per-session capacity. More work is not automatically more effective work. Ignoring exercise order, limiting useful range, or prioritizing comfort over the actual target can also reduce stimulus. At the opposite extreme, chronically very heavy loading, forced repetitions and beyond-failure work can spend recovery resources faster than they add benefit. Stable technique is part of the comparison. If the new record came from shorter range, more momentum or assistance, the log should not treat it as equivalent progression.

title: Progress without exhausting the runway — Key takeaways
text: Use stimulus and recovery observations together. Preserve a productive sequence of sessions instead of maximizing one session.

title: Recognize the cost of training — Local, systemic and axial fatigue
text: Fatigue is unavoidable; needless or excessive fatigue is manageable. Local fatigue affects the trained muscle and associated tissues. Systemic fatigue can reduce readiness and performance in muscles that were not directly trained. Axial fatigue arises from loading the spinal support structures; although local, it can limit many subsequent movements. A fatigued trunk may impair both rowing and squatting even when their primary targets differ. Useful signals include repeated performance losses, persistent connective-tissue irritation, unusually high perceived effort and reduced performance in otherwise unused muscles. Feeling tired alone is not enough to conclude that overload is impossible. The source gives comparable performance special weight, while acknowledging that perception and performance need interpretation together.

title: Recognize the cost of training — Fatigue can conceal adaptation
text: Fatigue is unavoidable; needless or excessive fatigue is manageable. A productive accumulation phase can create both more fitness and more fatigue. A temporary reduction in performance need not mean muscle was lost, and a performance jump after reduced training need not mean the reduced dose caused superior growth. Testing after comparable recovery conditions is more informative than comparing a fresh first week with a fatigued last week. However, this does not justify ignoring persistent deterioration. Repeated losses with overlapping soreness or joint irritation are reasons to change the plan. The goal is enough recoverability to continue good training, rather than either permanent exhaustion or a permanently pristine recovered state.

title: Recognize the cost of training — Key takeaways
text: Use several fatigue indicators, emphasizing comparable performance. Recovery is sufficient when useful training can continue; zero fatigue is not required.

title: Evaluate stimulus per fatigue cost — What the SFR represents
text: A high stimulus is useful only in the context of its costs. The stimulus-to-fatigue ratio (SFR) is conceptually hypertrophy stimulus ÷ fatigue generated . The book estimates stimulus with challenge, pump and muscle disruption, and fatigue with joint/connective-tissue disruption, perceived exertion and effects on unused-muscle performance. These ratings are informal proxies; their ratio is not a laboratory growth measurement. A chest-supported row may stimulate the back well while reducing trunk fatigue compared with an unsupported row. This does not make one version universally better: anthropometry, execution and the rest of the program change the comparison. Maximizing a ratio at a tiny dose also need not maximize total growth; enough useful total work is still necessary.

title: Evaluate stimulus per fatigue cost — Raise stimulus without needless spillover
text: A high stimulus is useful only in the context of its costs. Stable setup, controlled transitions, suitable range and targeting the intended muscles can improve the tradeoff without simply adding weight. Avoid momentum that shifts work away from the target or extra axial loading that does not serve the goal. Compound and isolation exercises can both have high or low SFR, depending on the person and situation. SFR generally worsens as very high volume or very low RIR creates disproportionately more fatigue. The source therefore balances effective work today with a second question: will this dose unnecessarily prevent planned progression later? A demanding set can be appropriate near the end of accumulation and inappropriate when it prematurely ends the whole sequence.

title: Evaluate stimulus per fatigue cost — Key takeaways
text: SFR is an informal comparison, not a physiological assay. Improve execution and exercise fit before automatically increasing dose.

title: Prevention, recovery sessions and deloads — Prevent avoidable fatigue
text: Match the scale of recovery intervention to the scale of fatigue. Stay within current volume landmarks, use safe technique and build pulsatility into the microcycle. Pulsatility means distributing demanding and easier exposures, rotating muscle priorities and managing overlapping trunk or synergist demands. It does not require a perfectly symmetric calendar. Rest days provide whole-body and psychological relief that splitting the same work into ever more days may not provide. The source often favors at least one full rest day weekly and deliberate rest over the year. These are author programming recommendations. Sleep and food support recovery but cannot compensate indefinitely for a workload beyond recoverable capacity.

title: Prevention, recovery sessions and deloads — Choose an appropriate reduction
text: Match the scale of recovery intervention to the scale of fatigue. Tool Intended role --- --- Recovery session Brief local reduction when fatigue disrupts an otherwise useful accumulation Deload A reduced-training microcycle for broader accumulated fatigue Active rest A longer low-stress break for persistent physical or psychological costs The source example halves sets and repetitions for a recovery session; a deload can also lower load later in the week. If 6 × 10 becomes 3 × 5 at the same load, tonnage falls to one quarter, not one half. The point is a substantial reduction, not a secret exact formula. Deload exercise choices can retain the prior exercises, introduce the next ones cautiously, or use low-fatigue alternatives.

title: Prevention, recovery sessions and deloads — Plan and adapt
text: Match the scale of recovery intervention to the scale of fatigue. Pre-plan safe technique, sensible dose and rest days. Autoregulate unanticipated recovery needs; repeated recovery sessions across many muscles suggest that a full deload may be more suitable than repeatedly patching local problems. Retain the feedback to improve the next plan. Do not reduce training solely because motivation is low, and do not ignore persistent joint pain simply because the muscle still performs. The book’s illness and injury examples describe coaching contexts, not diagnosis or medical clearance. Fever, significant injury and worsening symptoms require an appropriate clinical decision rather than treating a website exercise as rehabilitation.

title: Prevention, recovery sessions and deloads — Use the response to plan the return
text: Match the scale of recovery intervention to the scale of fatigue. After a recovery session caused by reaching MRV too soon, the book suggests returning to an intermediate volume between the starting effective dose and the prior limit, then progressing from response. After a temporary illness or minor resolved problem, it suggests a more modest reduction from the planned session rather than necessarily restarting the entire accumulation. These are different coaching scenarios, not interchangeable rules. Active rest is a broader reduction, commonly described as 1–4 weeks in the book, often shorter for physique-only psychological fatigue and longer when accumulated sporting stress warrants it. Short breaks may include no formal lifting; longer ones may use maintenance work. The authors discuss at least a full week away annually, often after a deload. These are source strategies, not a requirement that every recreational trainee calendar identical breaks. A performance-led review should also record whether symptoms are improving, stable or worsening. A recovery session is not established medical treatment, and the source itself conditions return-after-injury guidance on appropriate professional advice.

title: Prevention, recovery sessions and deloads — Key takeaways
text: Recovery interventions differ in scale and purpose. Prevention and feedback-based reductions complement each other.

title: Two clocks: recovery and growth — Do not collapse the two time courses
text: A useful model is not an exact biological stopwatch. A session stimulates adaptation and generates fatigue. The stimulus–recovery–adaptation (SRA) framework asks when another useful exposure can occur. Growth-related processes and restoration of performance are not the same curve; muscle can be stimulated to grow while fatigue remains, and a muscle that feels recovered is not necessarily still growing from the prior session. The authors describe growth often occurring over roughly 1–3 days while recovery can take longer in trained lifters. This is a conceptual source range, not a personalized forecast. Tissue type, exercise, dose, effort and training history alter the time course. A diagram with smooth curves cannot identify an exact optimal hour.

title: Two clocks: recovery and growth — Frequency distributes dose
text: A useful model is not an exact biological stopwatch. Weekly volume equals the sum of session volumes. Frequency is useful partly because it distributes hard sets into sessions that preserve stimulus quality. Twelve weekly sets in one session are not automatically equivalent to six sets on two days, especially if later sets in the long session become limited by technique, glycogen availability or systemic fatigue. Functional overreaching may be planned at the end of accumulation if followed by recovery; it does not license permanent under-recovery. Evaluate both per-session and weekly limits, since raising the recoverable weekly volume of one muscle can still exceed whole-body recovery capacity.

title: Two clocks: recovery and growth — Key takeaways
text: Recovery and adaptation have different time courses. Frequency is a way of distributing recoverable, useful work.

title: Why both extremes can fail — Too infrequent
text: More frequency solves some problems and creates others. Large infrequent sessions can produce excessive local damage, declining technique, weaker muscle awareness and systemic fatigue. Glycogen depletion and excitation–contraction limitations can further reduce later-set quality. More time between sessions is not a complete solution if each session creates unnecessarily large damage or if productive growth-related time is left unused. The source discusses a likely useful region around 3–8 sets per muscle per session and often 2–4 weekly exposures, with broad individual exceptions. These are starting ideas for trained lifters, not universal minimums or maximums. Study populations, failure definitions and whether weekly volume was equated affect interpretation.

title: Why both extremes can fail — Too frequent
text: More frequency solves some problems and creates others. Tiny highly frequent sessions repeat warm-ups and may lose the benefit of several sets for technical familiarity, target-muscle awareness and metabolite accumulation. Joint and connective tissues can recover more slowly than muscle; a frequency tolerated by muscle alone may therefore be unsustainable over months. Very frequent training can also raise weekly work until systemic recovery fails. Individual factors include muscle size, strength, fiber distribution, architecture, sex and the actual exercise used. Average group differences do not determine an individual’s schedule. Supporting muscles count too: spinal erectors, elbows or shoulder structures may be loaded across many nominally different muscle days.

title: Why both extremes can fail — Key takeaways
text: Neither maximum rest nor maximum frequency is automatically best. Track muscle, connective-tissue and systemic recovery together.

title: Derive a frequency from observations — A feedback loop
text: Use a repeatable experiment rather than a rigid muscle calendar. Begin with a plausible effective session dose near MEV. Observe when soreness and fatigue resolve, then compare performance at the next exposure. If performance cannot meet a comparable baseline, increase recovery or reduce the dose before assuming the muscle inherently needs a long interval. Starting far above MEV can falsely make every muscle seem slow to recover. A simpler source procedure starts with roughly twice-weekly exposures, progresses within recoverable volume and reviews the completed mesocycle. Consistently early recovery plus good performance can justify testing one more weekly exposure next mesocycle. Just-in-time recovery suggests holding frequency. Overlapping soreness and declining performance suggest less frequency, less dose, or a different exercise.

title: Derive a frequency from observations — An exercise can change the interval
text: Use a repeatable experiment rather than a rigid muscle calendar. Original comparison: a trainee recovers promptly from four leg-curl sets but remains disrupted after the same number of demanding hip-hinge sets. Equal set counts do not establish equal recovery demand. Changing the exercise mix can preserve a muscle’s weekly stimulus without forcing every exposure to be equally damaging. Document session dose, effort, soreness resolution, comparable performance and joint response. Revisit the schedule after the next mesocycle rather than changing everything after one unusual day. A workable real-life calendar with good recovery is preferable to a theoretically symmetric schedule that cannot be followed.

title: Derive a frequency from observations — An original frequency decision table
text: Use a repeatable experiment rather than a rigid muscle calendar. Repeated pattern Question to investigate Possible next experiment --- --- --- Early recovery and improving comparable performance Is there room for another useful exposure? Test a modest increase, keeping dose interpretable Recovery just in time and stable targets Is the present distribution already effective? Keep frequency while reviewing progression Overlapping soreness with performance loss Is dose, exercise damage or interval the problem? Reduce demands or extend recovery Muscle seems ready but joints stay irritated Are tissue time courses mismatched? Review loading, method and lower-stress phases This original table summarizes the source’s feedback logic without pretending to calculate a biological optimum. The source suggests deriving an interval across 2–5 consecutive exposures, or using a completed mesocycle for the simpler method, rather than drawing a conclusion from one session. Its theoretical frequency explanation includes muscle size and force, fiber-associated fatigue characteristics, architecture and stretch exposure, sex averages and whole-body demands. For example, a demanding lengthened hamstring hinge can have a different recovery cost from lateral-delt work. Such examples explain why to observe individual response; they do not identify a person’s fiber composition from soreness.

title: Derive a frequency from observations — Key takeaways
text: Dose and frequency must be tested together. Use repeated patterns and adjust modestly between mesocycles.

title: Change with a purpose — Adaptive resistance and repetitive stress
text: Directed variation preserves the goal; strategic variation chooses the moment. Variation intentionally changes training to reduce staleness or concentrated repetitive stress. Directed variation keeps the new stimulus aligned with the desired adaptation; strategic variation selects versions that suit the current phase. Randomly changing everything every week can sacrifice technical practice, comparable performance data and accumulated adaptation. The book lists exercise selection, movement speed, loading, volume, training method and order as possible levers. Change only what has a clear benefit. An exercise that continues to produce good stimulus, improving performance and tolerable joint response need not be replaced merely because a new month began.

title: Change with a purpose — Three replacement questions
text: Directed variation preserves the goal; strategic variation chooses the moment. Ask whether comparable performance has stalled, whether the exercise is producing accumulating joint or connective-tissue problems, and whether target-muscle stimulus has become stale. Several negative signs strengthen the case for replacement. Pain can justify action even while performance improves; high performance alone does not erase the cost. Avoid substituting a comfortable but less suitable exercise simply because the current one is demanding. Preplanned rotation can reduce biased decisions, while response-based changes preserve productive exercises longer. A new variation also needs a learning period before weak initial muscle awareness is treated as evidence that it does not suit the person.

title: Change with a purpose — Key takeaways
text: Variation should solve a defined problem. Retain effective movements; respond to staleness and accumulating tissue costs.

title: Compare stimulus, fatigue and time — Four comparison lenses
text: The limiting resource changes which exercise is useful. Lens Question --- --- RSM How much target stimulus does the exercise appear to provide? SFR How much stimulus for its fatigue cost? STR How much stimulus for the time spent? SFTR How do stimulus, fatigue and time costs combine? These are coaching comparison lenses, not precise biological units. When time is scarce, an efficient compound or superset may be attractive even if its fatigue cost is high. When a strong advanced lifter is recovery-limited, a supported or isolated movement may provide a better tradeoff. Compare the same person and target under reasonably similar conditions.

title: Compare stimulus, fatigue and time — Enough variety without fragmentation
text: The limiting resource changes which exercise is useful. The source commonly suggests around 1–3 exercises per muscle per session and 2–4 per week , interpreted as broad author guidelines. Too many exercises repeat setup and warm-up work, leave very few useful sets for each and can exhaust available variation prematurely. A movement with full appropriate range already recruits much of the target muscle; every session need not cover every imaginable angle. For example, two weekly sessions could share one reliable compound and each use one complementary isolation or alternate compound. Record which movement covers which action or regional emphasis. This is an original structure example, not a universal template or a promise that the listed exercise counts fit everyone.

title: Compare stimulus, fatigue and time — Key takeaways
text: Rank exercise tradeoffs relative to the current limiting resource. Avoid spending time on excessive setup instead of useful sets.

title: Coordinate load, tempo and order — Match the method to the movement
text: Variation must continue to serve specificity and overload. The book organizes loading into roughly 5–10, 10–20 and 20–30 repetition regions. No region fits every exercise equally well. Very high-repetition loaded hip hinges may be limited by breathing or trunk endurance, while very heavy isolation work can shift force away from the target or irritate joints. It is unnecessary to force all ranges into every session. Keep the same day’s exercise and range reasonably stable across accumulation for comparability. Controlled slower eccentrics or pauses can permit lower loads, improve technique or help reduce unwanted loading. They are not inherently superior growth tricks. Eccentric-accentuated loading is discussed as a potentially useful but uncertain tradeoff, with additional fatigue and implementation demands.

title: Coordinate load, tempo and order — Vary dose and order logically
text: Variation must continue to serve specificity and overload. Volume variation stays within current landmarks. A more axially fatiguing movement can receive fewer sets while a lower-fatigue complement receives more. Different loading ranges can be emphasized across days without replacing exercises weekly. Put priority muscles where they can receive quality work, and consider whether an early movement will fatigue a later movement’s limiting support structures. Adding drop sets, myoreps or supersets is justified by their specific role, such as time efficiency or target limitation. Exotic cadences, constant novelty and inappropriate load–exercise pairings can undermine higher-priority principles. Beginners generally gain more from learning a small reliable exercise set than from sophisticated weekly rotations.

title: Coordinate load, tempo and order — Key takeaways
text: Use varied ranges while preserving repeatable progression. New methods must earn their place in the plan.

title: Make today support tomorrow — Potentiation at several scales
text: Phase potentiation applies from repetitions to a training career. Phase potentiation arranges training so that a phase both works now and improves later training. It also prevents adaptive decay: gains should not be unnecessarily lost while another goal is pursued. At small scales, warm-up repetitions and well-managed sets prepare later work. At larger scales, a technical phase can prepare harder loading or a maintenance phase can prepare another productive growth block. Potentiation is not the claim that every preceding effort improves everything after it. A highly fatiguing trunk exercise before squats can do the opposite. Consider the target of the next exposure, the residual fatigue and which prior adaptations need maintenance.

title: Make today support tomorrow — Leave a path for next week
text: Phase potentiation applies from repetitions to a training career. The authors’ load-progression rule is to add only enough load that at least comparable repetitions remain possible at the same or slightly lower RIR. Their repetition rule mirrors this: add repetitions while retaining at least comparable load and the intended effort trajectory. The purpose is a productive sequence, often aiming for at least four accumulation weeks when appropriate. Large equipment increments need not force an early failure week. Accumulate repetitions within a sensible range before taking the next load jump. An unchanged load with more repetitions at comparable technique can be progression. Conversely, adding too much weight can reduce future sets and shorten the growth phase.

title: Make today support tomorrow — An original map across timescales
text: Phase potentiation applies from repetitions to a training career. Scale Preparation to preserve Cost to avoid --- --- --- Repetition to repetition Stable setup and practiced execution A poorly controlled rep that disrupts the next Exercise to exercise Warmth, readiness or deliberate target pre-fatigue Exhausting support muscles before the priority movement Week to week Enough overload and a viable next step Large jumps that end accumulation early Mesocycle to mesocycle Useful skill and retained muscle Carrying excessive fatigue into the next start Block or career Better limiting capacities and responsive training Repeatedly rebuilding gains that were needlessly lost This table is an original synthesis of the source’s small- and large-scale examples. A deliberately targeted pre-exhaust is distinct from accidentally exhausting a support structure: the former aims to make the intended muscle limit the next movement, while the latter prevents it from receiving sufficient work.

title: Make today support tomorrow — Key takeaways
text: Evaluate a phase by its present and future effects. Preserve comparable performance when increasing challenge.

title: Sequence mesocycles — Maintenance and resensitization
text: Changing emphasis is different from discarding every previous adaptation. Repeated high-volume mesocycles can increase required effective volume and work capacity while reducing sensitivity to a familiar dose. The book proposes lower-volume maintenance phases to reduce fatigue and restore responsiveness. This differs from a short deload: maintaining muscle at MV for several weeks is a larger strategic change than a brief fatigue reduction. The authors discuss approximately 3–6 weeks as a common maintenance/resensitization structure, while acknowledging uncertainty in exact durations and individual response. More is not automatically better; extending maintenance indefinitely also removes growth opportunities. Distinguish evidence, plausible mechanisms and the coach’s practical rule.

title: Sequence mesocycles — Shift emphasis rather than exclude ranges
text: Changing emphasis is different from discarding every previous adaptation. An author example gradually changes the shares of sets in low, moderate and high repetition ranges: 50/35/15%, then 25/50/25%, then 15/35/50%. All three shares sum to 100%. This illustrates a bias shift across mesocycles; it is not a superior ratio proven for every lifter. Retaining some exposure across ranges can avoid abrupt changes in fatigue and repeated recalibration. Heavier, lower-frequency emphasis may be followed by lighter, higher-frequency emphasis when appropriate, then a lower-stress phase. Exercise, cadence and supporting-muscle choices should fit each phase. The source warns against turning a nuanced sequence into 100% heavy, then 100% moderate, then 100% light work.

title: Sequence mesocycles — Key takeaways
text: Deload and maintenance phases serve different timescales. Use gradual emphasis shifts; preserve useful exposures.

title: Blocks, macrocycles and a career — Coordinate training and nutrition blocks
text: Long-term planning must retain flexibility and the right goal. The source describes sequences such as muscle gain, maintenance and fat loss, with training dose and nutrition aligned to the purpose. A lower-volume interval can reduce lingering fatigue before a new block. The exact number and duration of phases depend on the person, competition dates and response; the sequence is an example rather than a mandatory annual template. Frequent switching between short gain and loss phases can sacrifice consistent adaptation and create repeated transitions. At macrocycle scale, identify a limiting muscle or movement skill and prepare it deliberately. Changing splits gradually lets prior experience remain informative rather than resetting every variable at once.

title: Blocks, macrocycles and a career — Build the foundation first
text: Long-term planning must retain flexibility and the right goal. The authors summarize a career emphasis as basic technique → relative effort → mind–muscle connection . This ordering does not mean beginners should train without awareness or advanced lifters can neglect technique. It means later refinements depend on safe, repeatable execution and an ability to estimate effort. Excessive resensitization, unnecessary strength phases or perpetual leanness can conflict with a primary hypertrophy goal. These may still be valid personal choices. State their opportunity costs clearly and judge the plan against the person’s actual goals, rather than assuming every choice must maximize muscle growth.

title: Blocks, macrocycles and a career — Key takeaways
text: Plan for retained gains and future opportunities. Foundational technique makes later refinement possible.

title: Why the same plan produces different responses — Sources of variation
text: Individualization changes application, not the underlying need for sound principles. Work capacity is the ability to perform work; recovery ability is the ability to restore function between exposures. They are related but not interchangeable. Anthropometry affects leverage and which muscles limit an exercise. Fiber characteristics, initial muscle size, adaptive response, age, training history, sleep, nutrition and life stress all influence useful training choices. The book also discusses genetic influences on muscle shape and growth potential. They do not let a simple visual assessment predict a person’s final ceiling, nor can an exercise transform the underlying attachment anatomy. Different muscles in the same person can respond differently. Use group averages as starting hypotheses, then observe the individual.

title: Why the same plan produces different responses — Learn from one person over time
text: Individualization changes application, not the underlying need for sound principles. Individualize volume landmarks, exercise choice, progression, frequency and phase length by repeated feedback. A useful log records execution, load, reps, RIR, stimulus impressions, fatigue, sleep and relevant context. If the environment changes, prior landmarks are hypotheses rather than permanent facts. Do not label every inconvenient exercise unsuitable for your body. New movements may need time for technique and awareness to develop. On the other hand, copying a professional’s plan or a training partner’s dose ignores their different recovery and experience. Make small informative changes so their effects can be interpreted.

title: Why the same plan produces different responses — An original response-and-confound map
text: Individualization changes application, not the underlying need for sound principles. Observation Possible contribution Do not conclude automatically --- --- --- More repetitions across several sets Work capacity, skill or fatigue differences Faster between-session recovery Fast early growth Initial size, responsiveness or beginner status The highest final growth ceiling A different response in later years Training age and changed circumstances The newer method caused the entire difference A muscle favors one exercise Anatomy, execution and local response The same exercise is best for every muscle A sex-group average differs Group-level traits and typical loading Every individual needs the group-average schedule The source distinguishes initial muscle size, gain rate, response per unit stimulus and long-term potential. They are related but not interchangeable. A fair personal experiment also considers diet, sleep, stress and training-age changes. The authors discuss spending a block biased toward one repetition range while retaining some others, then comparing several indicators. Such an experiment remains observational; changing one emphasis does not perfectly isolate a cellular pathway.

title: Why the same plan produces different responses — Key takeaways
text: Work capacity and recovery capacity are different. Repeated feedback refines general principles for a particular person.

title: Beginner, intermediate and advanced decisions — Beginners need a technical foundation
text: Experience changes the useful complexity and recovery costs. The source favors broad whole-body development and a small number of reliable exercises for beginners. Add load when technique remains at least as good and effort stays under control; the author checklist uses approximately 2 or more RIR. Early rapid strength increases should not outrun movement quality. Beginners can often grow with low volumes and do not usually require specialization, elaborate metabolite methods or constant exercise replacement. A few weekly full-body sessions can provide repeated skill practice without excessive gym attendance. These are source programming patterns, not a classification test based only on years since joining a gym.

title: Beginner, intermediate and advanced decisions — As the lifter becomes more developed
text: Experience changes the useful complexity and recovery costs. Intermediates often need more deliberate set progression, broader repetition ranges and improved SFR. As strength rises, previously tolerable compounds may generate enough systemic fatigue to require alternatives. Deloads and strategic low-volume periods become more relevant. Advanced lifters may need very precise muscle-specific dose, more careful joint management and specialization. Greater local demands can exceed systemic resources before every muscle receives its best growth work. More sessions are not a badge of advancement: their value depends on whether they preserve useful performance, recovery and a sustainable life schedule. Advanced refinements do not remove the need for consistent technique and honest effort assessment.

title: Beginner, intermediate and advanced decisions — Key takeaways
text: Progress technical competence before adding complexity. Greater development often makes recovery management more important.

title: Diet phases and specialization — The adaptive window changes
text: Recovery conditions determine how much useful work can be supported. The book’s model proposes a wider MEV–MRV window during a calorie surplus and a narrower one during a deficit. Recovery and growth are more constrained during fat loss, and maintaining muscle becomes the relevant success criterion, especially for trained lifters. Do not interpret a smaller window as permission to compensate with unlimited extra effort. At maintenance, a low-volume resensitization phase may be appropriate when that is the planned goal. During fat loss, the authors often favor high-SFR choices and cautious progression as fatigue increases. Exact landmark shifts cannot be calculated from calorie balance alone. Record the person’s actual performance and tissue response rather than assigning automatic set changes.

title: Diet phases and specialization — Prioritize some muscles and maintain others
text: Recovery conditions determine how much useful work can be supported. Specialization trains priority muscles for growth while holding others near maintenance. It can solve a systemic bottleneck when every muscle cannot simultaneously receive a productive growth dose. Because MV is often substantially below MEV in trained lifters, lowering non-priority work can free meaningful resources while preserving prior gains. Do not leave non-priority muscles at a vague in-between dose that adds fatigue without robust growth, or neglect them below maintenance. Rotate priorities deliberately and allow the priority muscles low-stress periods too. The source does not generally recommend growth specialization during a deficit, where growth opportunities are already limited. Beginners usually do not need this strategy.

title: Diet phases and specialization — Key takeaways
text: A fat-loss phase changes both the goal and the recovery context. Specialization reallocates resources while preserving other muscles.

title: Audit a stalled program — A principles-first audit
text: Troubleshoot the whole framework before changing one favorite variable. Check specificity first: is the target muscle actually trained in a growth-promoting way? Then inspect dose, effort and progression, followed by fatigue, frequency, variation and phase structure. A complex schedule cannot rescue insufficient stimulus, while harder training cannot solve chronic under-recovery. The source’s troubleshooting list also includes nutrition, sleep, consistent execution, resensitization where appropriate, patience and realistic expectations. Compare performance under similar conditions across mesocycles. Muscular change is often too slow and measurement error too large to interpret day-to-day fluctuations as tissue gain or loss.

title: Audit a stalled program — Evidence that can and cannot establish progress
text: Troubleshoot the whole framework before changing one favorite variable. Rep strength over several well-executed mesocycles is useful indirect evidence, but skill and altered execution confound it. Pump, RSM and SFR support decisions about the training process rather than proving final growth. Photographs and circumference measures require consistent conditions; body-composition tools have their own precision limits. Original audit example: a trainee reports a plateau after two weeks but has changed exercises, increased momentum and weighed in at different times. First standardize the comparison and continue an appropriate observation period. Do not automatically add volume to solve an apparent plateau that the records cannot yet establish.

title: Audit a stalled program — Key takeaways
text: Investigate fundamentals in order of importance. Standardize measurements and allow an appropriate timescale.

title: Train within time and risk constraints — When time is limited
text: A useful compromise should make its costs visible. The source suggests prioritizing efficient compounds, reducing setup and warm-up transitions, using suitable antagonist supersets and applying short-rest isolation methods where local fatigue remains the limiter. A fixed modest set count may be more feasible than a large weekly volume ramp. Advanced lifters with little time may benefit from prioritizing fewer muscles while maintaining others. This is a stimulus-to-time tradeoff, not a way to obtain unlimited results in minimal time. Shorter rest can become counterproductive when breathing or supporting muscles terminate work too soon. The authors discuss lower RIR when total dose is very low, but fatigue, technical control and exercise safety remain relevant.

title: Train within time and risk constraints — Conservative training and return after injury
text: A useful compromise should make its costs visible. The source’s cautious-training examples reduce load, avoid abrupt directional changes, use controlled tempo and stable equipment, progress conservatively and stop accumulation before extreme fatigue. They deliberately trade some potential growth for a lower-demand approach. Lower demand does not mean zero risk, and a website cannot diagnose why a movement hurts. The book sketches return after injury as a progression from completed rehabilitation through tolerable local work, restored movement range, compound reintroduction and gradual loading. It also discusses blood-flow restriction in that context. These are source concepts, not a self-directed rehabilitation protocol: injury type, contraindications, equipment and clinician guidance determine what is appropriate. Do not infer clearance from a quiz score or calculator.

title: Train within time and risk constraints — An original map of the source’s return concept
text: A useful compromise should make its costs visible. Source stage Educational purpose --- --- Complete prescribed rehabilitation Establish clinical readiness before gym progression Consider suitably supervised light local work Reintroduce a tolerable stimulus where appropriate Restore range with local training Recover controlled movement through the permitted range Reintroduce compounds Integrate previously isolated capacity into larger movements Gradually restore loading Test increasing demand without rushing the transition Resume normal training Continue individualized monitoring rather than assume permanent immunity This is a conceptual map of the book’s six-stage discussion, not its protocol reproduced as instructions. The source’s optional blood-flow-restriction stage only applies where anatomically and clinically appropriate. The authors also explicitly say not to follow the book against a medical professional’s advice or when it causes pain at the injury site. A fixed timetable cannot establish that a particular injury is ready.

title: Train within time and risk constraints — Key takeaways
text: Time-saving methods need an appropriate limiting factor. Medical recovery concepts are not personal clearance or a rehabilitation prescription.

title: Fit hypertrophy around cardio and sport — Cardio compatibility is dose-dependent
text: The sport’s needs analysis decides how muscle growth fits. The source discusses potential interference from energy use, local fatigue, connective-tissue loading, training time and competing signaling. It also recognizes that some conditioning can help otherwise sedentary trainees tolerate lifting and that cardiovascular work serves goals beyond maximum hypertrophy. Do not interpret the interference discussion as a reason to avoid all aerobic activity. The authors generally favor less fatiguing, lower-impact options when muscle growth is primary, and separating sessions where feasible. Their specific heart-rate and duration examples are general coaching heuristics, not individualized safety limits. Evaluate whether cardio is reducing actual lifting quality and recovery rather than assuming every bout has an identical negative effect.

title: Fit hypertrophy around cardio and sport — Sport performance has the final priority
text: The sport’s needs analysis decides how muscle growth fits. For an athlete, more muscle is useful only when it supports the sport’s body-composition, strength-to-mass, force–velocity, skill and tactical needs. Added mass can be useful in one context and costly in another. Hypertrophy also has an opportunity cost: fatigue and time spent gaining size can reduce skill practice or competition readiness. The source often emphasizes compound work in a 5–10 repetition region with intentional force production for strength/power sports, while reducing other demands to accommodate it. This differs from physique-only training. Consolidating demanding sessions on the same day, separated when appropriate, can preserve true recovery days; merely placing every activity on a different day can eliminate them. Exact scheduling remains sport- and athlete-dependent.

title: Fit hypertrophy around cardio and sport — Context changes the sequencing advice
text: The sport’s needs analysis decides how muscle growth fits. The book gives different ordering examples in different contexts. Its cardio-and-hypertrophy section suggests separating sessions and, when combined, discusses cardio before lifting with a signaling rationale. Its sport-integration section instead prioritizes lifting before cardiovascular work during a hypertrophy-priority phase to preserve overload. The course does not erase this tension or convert either into a universal rule. The relevant decision is phase priority, actual performance, fatigue and feasibility. The source’s sport example reduces a muscle’s usual weekly exposure by roughly 0.5–1 session: the half-session example means retaining one lighter exposure, not doing half a calendar visit. It also describes separating demanding same-day sessions by 4–8 hours where feasible to consolidate stressors and preserve recovery days. These are author examples rather than personalized timing prescriptions. Non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT), such as walking and household activity, is another source topic: daily movement can contribute energy expenditure with different fatigue costs from demanding cardio. A sharp decline in ordinary activity during a deficit is relevant context for recovery and energy review, not a diagnostic test.

title: Fit hypertrophy around cardio and sport — Key takeaways
text: Account for dose, overlap and the athlete’s actual goals. More muscle is not automatically better sporting performance.

title: Hypertrophy training
text: muscle growth Training that directly promotes muscle growth or retention in a deficit, or develops capacities that support later growth. The purpose distinguishes it from testing maximal strength.

title: Exercise
text: A named movement pattern used to stimulate a muscle or group of muscles. Different exercises can overlap in their target and supporting structures.

title: Repetition
text: rep One execution from the intended starting point through the intended range and back, with the required technical standard. A changed range changes the comparison.

title: Set
text: A collection of relatively continuous repetitions, separated from other sets by rest. Set counts are useful only when execution, effort and loading context are understood.

title: Training session
text: A dedicated period of training, normally including warm-up and one or more exercises. Session frequency and a muscle’s exposure frequency need not be identical.

title: Rest time
text: rest interval Time allowed for fatigue to dissipate between repetitions, sets, exercises or sessions. The relevant systems must recover sufficiently for the intended next task.

title: One-repetition maximum
text: 1RM The greatest external load that can be lifted once in a particular exercise under a defined execution standard. It is exercise-specific, not a universal whole-body capacity.

title: Microcycle
text: The shortest repeated cycle that includes the planned sessions and rest days. It is commonly, but not necessarily, one week.

title: Mesocycle
text: An organized sequence of microcycles directed toward related adaptations; in the source it commonly contains accumulation followed by a shorter deload.

title: Accumulation phase
text: Successive microcycles in which the training challenge rises through a managed combination of sets, repetitions, load or effort.

title: Deload
text: deload phase A reduced-training microcycle intended to lower accumulated fatigue while preserving adaptations. It differs in scale from one recovery session.

title: Accumulation-to-deload paradigm
text: The relationship between time spent accumulating and time spent deloading in a mesocycle. More productive accumulation relative to necessary recovery can improve training continuity.

title: Training block
text: One or more mesocycles sharing a unified goal, such as gaining muscle or losing fat while preserving muscle.

title: Macrocycle
text: A sequence of training blocks organized around a long-term goal. Its exact duration follows the purpose rather than necessarily matching a calendar year.

title: Periodization
text: The deliberate sequencing of training variables and phases to support adaptation, manage fatigue and prepare performance when needed.

title: Autoregulation
text: Adjusting training variables or fatigue management in response to actual needs rather than only following predetermined changes. It uses interpreted feedback, not momentary preference alone.

title: Volume
text: hard-set volume The quantity of work performed over a defined interval. In this hypertrophy framework, useful hard sets per muscle per session or week are the usual practical proxy.

title: Load
text: absolute intensity The absolute external resistance used in an exercise. It does not by itself describe the effort required from a particular person.

title: Relative load
text: %1RM Load expressed relative to maximal capacity for the same exercise, commonly as a percentage of 1RM: load divided by 1RM, multiplied by 100%.

title: Relative effort
text: How demanding a set is relative to current capability. The source uses RIR to express effort; it is separate from relative loading.

title: Repetitions in reserve
text: RIR reps from failure An estimate of additional full, technically acceptable repetitions possible at the end of a set. Zero RIR means another complete acceptable repetition cannot be performed.

title: Frequency
text: training frequency The number of sessions or muscle exposures per unit of time. Specify which is counted; weekly gym visits and exposures for a given muscle can differ.

title: Maintenance volume
text: MV The amount of training sufficient to prevent loss of current muscle under the relevant conditions. It is not necessarily enough to stimulate robust new growth.

title: Minimum effective volume
text: MEV The estimated training dose at which robust growth begins. It varies with the person, muscle, training history, exercise and current circumstances.

title: Maximum adaptive volume
text: MAV The currently most productive volume region for growth. In the source framework it is a moving region, not a fixed universal set number.

title: Maximum recoverable volume
text: MRV The upper training-volume region beyond which recovery no longer supports sustained productive training. Local and systemic limits can differ.

title: Fatigue
text: Acute or accumulated reduction in performance capacity arising from physical and psychological stressors. It can be local, systemic or related to axial loading.

title: Overreaching
text: functional overreaching A state where accumulated fatigue prevents sustained overload. Planned functional overreaching is followed by recovery; unintended prolonged under-recovery is not the same strategy.

title: Minicut
text: A relatively short, more aggressive fat-loss interval intended to prepare later muscle gain or temporarily change appearance, rather than serve as a long-term dieting pattern.

title: Muscle-gain phase
text: massing A training and nutrition period with a muscle-growth goal, commonly using a calorie surplus in the source framework. The surplus does not specify a personal diet.

title: Fat-loss phase
text: cutting A calorie-deficit period aimed at reducing body fat while retaining muscle. Recovery and growth opportunities differ from those in a surplus.

title: Weight-maintenance phase
text: A period with approximately stable body mass and energy balance. It may be paired with lower-volume training when recovery or resensitization is the goal.

title: Resensitization phase
text: A lower-volume period, often near maintenance volume, intended to lower fatigue and adaptive resistance before more productive future training. Exact optimal duration remains uncertain.

title: Stimulus-to-fatigue ratio
text: SFR A conceptual comparison of relevant training stimulus with fatigue cost. The source’s subjective scores are informal coaching proxies rather than direct measurements of muscle growth.

title: Raw stimulus magnitude
text: RSM The source’s estimate of target-muscle stimulus from challenge, pump and disruption. It is person- and muscle-specific and does not prove subsequent hypertrophy.

title: Stimulus–recovery–adaptation
text: SRA A framework linking a training exposure with fatigue reduction and adaptation before another productive exposure. Growth and performance recovery need not follow identical clocks.

title: Range of motion
text: ROM The excursion used in an exercise. In this source, useful full range is limited by effective targeting, technical control and tolerability rather than forcing maximal excursion at any cost.

title: Variation
text: Intentional changes in training variables that address adaptive resistance or repetitive stress while remaining aligned with the target adaptation.

title: Specificity
text: The principle that training should directly improve the desired outcome or prepare capacities that support it. It guides the meaning of useful overload.

title: Phase potentiation
text: Purposeful sequencing so that current training also prepares more effective subsequent training while avoiding unnecessary loss of prior adaptations.

title: Stimulus-to-time ratio
text: STR The source’s comparison of estimated stimulus with total time required for setup, warm-up, sets and associated rest. It is a contextual efficiency heuristic.

title: Stimulus–fatigue–time ratio
text: SFTR A combined exercise-selection lens considering estimated stimulus alongside fatigue and time costs. It is not a standardized physiological measurement.

title: Load, effort and work — Three numbers, three meanings
text: Load and effort are separate variables. The book uses intensity for the external resistance, commonly reported as the mass on the bar in kg or lb. Its term relative intensity means proximity to concentric failure. This differs from the convention that calls percentage of one-repetition maximum “relative intensity.” Always name the convention in a training log. A heavy single with several repetitions available can use more load but less effort than a lighter set taken near failure. Frequency counts training exposures per stated time unit. “Three sessions per week” does not specify their exercises, difficulty or distribution. Exercise selection identifies the actual movement; “legs” is not a reproducible exercise prescription.

title: Load, effort and work — Volume is a comparison tool
text: Load and effort are separate variables. For repeated identical lifts, the book uses volume load as a convenient proxy: Volume load = sets × repetitions × load (kg·repetitions). This is not mechanical work in joules. Work also requires displacement and force; kilograms describe mass, not force. If the same lifter performs 4 × 5 × 100 kg, the proxy is 2,000 kg·repetitions. A different range of motion, exercise, machine leverage or lifter changes its meaning. Thus equal tonnage in curls and deadlifts does not imply equal stimulus or fatigue. Record exercise, range, effort and rest alongside volume; compare like with like.

title: Load, effort and work — Key takeaways
text: Load and effort are separate variables. Volume load omits displacement and is meaningful mainly within comparable lifts.

title: Load, effort and work — Volume-load laboratory
text: Compare the arithmetic of sets, repetitions and load. Inputs: sets, repetitions, external mass in kg. Output: sets × repetitions × kg, reported as kg·repetitions. Change one input at a time. Same lift, lifter and range of motion; mass proxy only. This does not estimate biological stimulus, calories, fatigue or injury risk. Positive finite inputs; reset restores the example. 4 sets × 5 repetitions × 100 kg = 2,000 kg·repetitions. Halving load halves this proxy if everything else stays fixed. Verified by direct multiplication: 4 × 5 × 100 = 2,000; 2 × 5 × 100 = 1,000; doubling any one factor doubles the output.

title: From a session to a macrocycle — Nested planning units
text: Planning units are defined by training purpose. A session is one bout with a beginning and end. A microcycle spans the recurrence of a session type, often a week but not necessarily seven days. An accumulation phase comprises progressively demanding microcycles. A deload is a microcycle of substantially easier work intended to reduce fatigue while retaining adaptations. A mesocycle organizes microcycles toward a distinct adaptation, often accumulation followed by deload. A block groups one or more mesocycles sharing a purpose. A macrocycle orders blocks toward a larger outcome, often a competition. These units describe function; calendar length alone does not determine the unit.

title: From a session to a macrocycle — Training and nutrition are different axes
text: Planning units are defined by training purpose. Hypertrophy, basic strength and peaking name training goals. Mass gain, maintenance and cutting name body-mass or nutritional goals. They interact but are not synonyms. A hypertrophy-style block can be used to retain muscle during a cut; a maintenance diet can accompany several training goals. An illustrative macrocycle is muscle development → strength development → peaking → competition → active rest. Active rest deliberately lacks an accumulation phase. A 3:1 accumulation-to-deload ratio means three units of accumulation for one of deload, not that every athlete must use four-week months. All lengths must remain compatible with recovery and the competition calendar.

title: From a session to a macrocycle — Planning and measurement map
text: Planning units are defined by training purpose. Quantity What to record A common mistaken inference --- --- --- External load kg or lb, including the bar A heavier bar always means a harder set Failure proximity Repetitions still possible under the stated conditions The same %1RM means the same effort Volume load Sets × repetitions × kg Equal tonnage means equal adaptation across lifts Frequency Exposures per named interval More sessions always means more weekly work Microcycle Recurrence of a session pattern Every microcycle must be exactly seven days Block goal Development plus preservation Nutrition and training phase names are interchangeable A hypothetical lifter logs 100 kg × 8 with two repetitions available, then later 102.5 kg × 8 with the same reserve and range. That is interpretable load progression. If the second set instead uses shortened range or reaches failure, several variables changed. Record that difference before comparing. The purpose of measurement is to preserve the meaning of the comparison, not merely collect a larger number.

title: From a session to a macrocycle — Key takeaways
text: Planning units are defined by training purpose. Nutritional phases and training blocks should not be confused.

title: Capacity, technique and mobility — General capacity and the limiting point
text: Task-specific performance depends on the limiting portion. Strength is maximal force-producing capacity. Task-specific strength is that capacity expressed in a particular movement under its constraints. A deadlift that can be locked out from blocks with 250 kg but can only be initiated from the floor with 200 kg is limited to a 200 kg full lift. Partial-range ability does not establish full-range competition ability. Technique organizes positions and movement to use available force effectively. Body proportions alter feasible positions, but individualization does not remove the need to satisfy competition standards or maintain controlled execution. Practice must address the actual limiting portion rather than only the strongest portion.

title: Capacity, technique and mobility — Mobility is more than stretching
text: Task-specific performance depends on the limiting portion. The book defines mobility as the intersection of flexibility, strength and technique. Flexibility permits a range of motion; strength supports positions; technique supplies the coordination and knowledge to use them. A lifter who can reach squat depth unloaded but cannot maintain position under a manageable load may not have a flexibility-only problem. Use an assessment question rather than an automatic intervention: Is the missing position unavailable, unsupported, or not yet learned? This model is a conceptual distinction, not a diagnosis.
